The notebooks below accompany Unit 6. They are ordinary Jupyter
notebooks and need only `numpy` (plus `matplotlib` for the plots, and
`control`/`slycot` for some of the continuous-time models); open them in
JupyterLab, VS Code, or any notebook environment. A dependency-free
Python implementation of the filter itself is in
[`kalman_filter.py`](kalman_filter.py) -- see [`README.md`](README.md).

## Linear quadratic control with stochastic disturbances

The first half of the unit, made concrete: the finite-horizon LQ
controller applied to a plant driven by random disturbances. Two things
are worth watching. The controller copes with the disturbances without
any modification -- this is certainty equivalence, the optimal gains
being the deterministic ones -- and the expected cost predicted by the
theory, $x_0^\intercal P_0x_0+\sum_k\text{trace}(P_{k+1}W)$, matches the
average cost over Monte Carlo runs. That second check is the one to run
yourself: it turns an identity on the page into a number.

[Download `A_6_LQCstochastic.ipynb`](A_6_LQCstochastic.ipynb){download="A_6_LQCstochastic.ipynb"}

## The Kalman filter

The filter itself, iterated on a worked example for long enough that the
gains converge to their stationary values, and then checked against the
library routine. Running it is the quickest way to see the point made in
the notes: the covariances $\Phi_{k|k-1}$, $\Phi_{k|k}$ and the gain
$L_k$ do not depend on the measurements at all, so they can be computed
offline before any data arrives.

[Download `A_6_Kalman.ipynb`](A_6_Kalman.ipynb){download="A_6_Kalman.ipynb"}

## LQG control of an inverted pendulum

The separation principle at work on the inverted pendulum of Unit 5,
which here must be controlled from a single noisy measurement rather than
the full state. The average-cost infinite-horizon LQG controller is
assembled from the two dual Riccati equations -- the LQR gain and the
stationary Kalman gain, designed independently -- and the comparison
against Unit 5's full-state response shows exactly what partial
information costs.

[Download `A_6_lqg.ipynb`](A_6_lqg.ipynb){download="A_6_lqg.ipynb"}

## Sensor fusion: lidar and accelerometer on a mass-spring-damper

An object on a spring carries two sensors: a lidar measuring distance to
a wall, and an accelerometer. Neither alone gives a good position
estimate -- the lidar is noisy, the accelerometer drifts when integrated
twice -- but the Kalman filter merges them into one estimate that is
better than either, and an LQG controller is then built on top. This is
sensor fusion in its most recognizable form, and the clearest argument
for why the filter is worth the algebra.

[Download `A_6_K_SensorFusionAndLQG.ipynb`](A_6_K_SensorFusionAndLQG.ipynb){download="A_6_K_SensorFusionAndLQG.ipynb"}

## IMU pose estimation: Kalman versus complementary filter

An inertial measurement unit combines gyroscopes, accelerometers and
magnetometers: the gyroscope measures angular velocity, while the
accelerometer and magnetometer together yield the attitude angles. With
the kinematics linearized the three angles decouple, so each is a small
estimation problem. The notebook compares the Kalman filter against the
*complementary* filter, the fixed-gain scheme widely used on embedded
hardware, which is the practical question an engineer actually faces: is
the extra machinery worth it here?

[Download `A_6_K_KalmanIMU.ipynb`](A_6_K_KalmanIMU.ipynb){download="A_6_K_KalmanIMU.ipynb"}

## A min-max game against a worst-case disturbance

The same linear plant and quadratic cost as the rest of the unit, but
with the disturbance $\omega_k$ no longer a sequence of independent
Gaussian variables: here it is chosen *adversarially*, to make the cost
as large as the controller tries to make it small. The problem becomes a
min-max game rather than a minimization, and the question is what
survives of the Riccati machinery when the uncertainty stops being random
and starts pushing back.

[Download `A_6_K_quadraticgame.ipynb`](A_6_K_quadraticgame.ipynb){download="A_6_K_quadraticgame.ipynb"}
